summary: This informational document records the transfer of responsibility for several Ethernet-related MIB modules, including EtherLike-MIB and MAU-MIB, from the IETF to the IEEE 802.3 Working Group.

eli5.summary: A set of network meter definitions had one owner, and now another group looks after them. This is the note that records that handover.

questions: why did ietf transfer mib modules
subtitle: Recording the transfer of Ethernet MIB modules from IETF to IEEE 802.3

tldr.problem: Eight Ethernet-related MIB (Management Information Base) modules that define how to monitor and manage Ethernet devices were originally developed and maintained by the IETF but are more appropriately maintained by the IEEE 802.3 Working Group, which defines the Ethernet standard.
tldr.mechanism: The IETF formally transfers responsibility for DOT3-OAM-MIB, SNMP-REPEATER-MIB, POWER-ETHERNET-MIB, DOT3-EPON-MIB, EtherLike-MIB, EFM-CU-MIB, ETHER-WIS, and MAU-MIB to IEEE 802.3, mirroring a similar transfer of bridge-related modules to IEEE 802.1 done in RFC 4663.
tldr.outcome: The IEEE 802.3 group now maintains these modules, publishes them in IEEE 802.3.1-2013, assigns OIDs under the IEEE branch, and manages all future updates. This aligns standards governance with the technical domain of expertise.

today: RFC 7448 is an Informational document recording a completed organizational transfer. It is not obsoleted. The transferred MIB modules are now maintained by IEEE 802.3 as part of the IEEE 802.3.1 standard.

sections.title: The Transfer of MIB Modules
sections.content:
This document records the transfer of responsibility for eight Ethernet-related MIB modules from the IETF to the IEEE 802.3 Working Group. MIB modules are standardized definitions that describe how to monitor and manage network equipment using the Simple Network Management Protocol (SNMP).

The transfer follows the same pattern established by RFC 4663, which transferred bridge-related MIB modules from the IETF to IEEE 802.1. Because the IEEE 802.3 group develops and maintains the core Ethernet standard, it is the most appropriate home for MIBs that describe Ethernet devices.

The transfer was completed years before this RFC was published; the document's purpose is to formally record the completed transfer and clarify governance and maintenance responsibilities going forward.
sections.eli5: The group that maintains the Ethernet standard (IEEE 802.3) is now responsible for keeping these management definitions up to date. This RFC just records that change so everyone knows who to ask.

sections.title: The Eight Transferred Modules
sections.content:
The eight modules transferred from IETF to IEEE 802.3 are:

DOT3-OAM-MIB (from RFC 4878): Defines objects for Operations, Administration, and Maintenance (OAM) functions on Ethernet-like interfaces.

SNMP-REPEATER-MIB (from RFC 2108): Defines managed objects for IEEE 802.3 repeater devices.

POWER-ETHERNET-MIB (from RFC 3621): Defines objects for Power over Ethernet, which supplies electrical power to devices over network cables.

DOT3-EPON-MIB (from RFC 4837): Defines managed objects for Ethernet Passive Optical Networks, fiber-optic Ethernet systems.

EtherLike-MIB (from RFC 3635): Defines objects for Ethernet-like interface types, a broad management standard.

EFM-CU-MIB (from RFC 5066): Defines interfaces for Ethernet in the First Mile Copper, used for short-distance copper-based Ethernet.

ETHER-WIS (from RFC 3637): Defines objects for the Ethernet WAN Interface Sublayer, used for long-distance Ethernet over optical networks.

MAU-MIB (from RFC 4836): Defines objects for Medium Attachment Units (MAUs), the physical connectors and interfaces on Ethernet devices.

All eight modules are now published as part of IEEE 802.3.1-2013 and maintained by IEEE 802.3.
sections.eli5: Eight different instruction sets for managing Ethernet gear are now under IEEE 802.3's control. They cover everything from repeaters to fiber optics to power supplies.

sections.title: Prior Transfers and Precedent
sections.content:
This transfer follows the same pattern established by RFC 4663, which in 2006 transferred responsibility for four bridge-related MIB modules from the IETF to IEEE 802.1. The success of that transfer demonstrates the benefits of aligning standards governance with technical expertise.

The bridge MIB transfer occurred because IEEE 802.1 is the standards body responsible for defining bridge functionality, making it the logical home for bridge management definitions. Similarly, IEEE 802.3 is the standards body for Ethernet, making it the most appropriate maintainer of Ethernet-related MIBs.

Both transfers reflect a broader principle in standards development: technical governance should reside with the organization that owns the core technology standard. This alignment improves responsiveness to technical changes, coordinates protocol development with management interface definitions, and reduces duplication of effort.
sections.eli5: A similar transfer happened to bridge management definitions a few years earlier, and it worked well. Now Ethernet management is moving the same way.

sections.title: Governance and Maintenance Procedures
sections.content:
The transfer includes several procedural elements:

ASCII format publication: IEEE publishes MIB modules in ASCII format on its public website, making them available for operators and vendors to download and use.

OID registration: New MIB modules developed by IEEE 802.3 use Object Identifiers (OIDs) assigned under the IEEE branch of the OID tree, not the IETF branch. Information about IEEE registration arcs is published at http://www.ieee802.org/3/arcs/index.html.

Mailing list and discussion: The Ethernet Interfaces and Hub MIB Working Group, which developed these modules, closed in September 2007. Future discussions about IEEE 802.3 MIB modules should occur on the IEEE list STDS-802-3-MIB@LISTSERV.IEEE.ORG.

IETF MIB Doctor reviews: When new Ethernet MIB modules are submitted to the IETF, they still receive MIB Doctor review (a quality gate by IETF experts). References to "802.1" in such reviews should be understood as applying to "802.3" for these modules.
sections.eli5: IEEE 802.3 now owns these definitions, publishes them, assigns ID numbers to new ones, and manages a mailing list for discussion. The IETF still reviews them for quality before they are published.

references.text: Harrington, D., "Transferring MIB Work from IETF Bridge MIB WG to IEEE 802.1 WG", RFC 4663, September 2006.
